**Accuracy ignores confidence once the winning class is chosen; cross-entropy does not.** A prediction with correct-class probability 0.51 and one with 0.99 can both count as correct, while assigning probability 0.01 to a true class is punished much more than assigning 0.4. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)

**A small example explains the divergence.** Imagine 100 validation examples. The model corrects one borderline mistake, improving accuracy by one percentage point. But on two remaining mistakes it becomes dramatically more confident in the wrong class, reducing their true-class probabilities from 0.1 to 0.0001. Each of those examples adds roughly $\log(1000)$ nats of extra loss, which can outweigh the gain from the corrected example.

Thus increasing accuracy and increasing validation cross-entropy are compatible. The model may be improving decision boundaries slightly while worsening probability calibration or overfitting a few difficult/noisy cases.

Inspect the per-example loss distribution, confidence on errors, label quality, and calibration curves. Do not assume the average loss trend is a logging bug, but verify train/eval settings and dataset consistency too.

Choose checkpointing according to the deployment objective. If calibrated probabilities matter for risk or ranking, accuracy alone is insufficient. Temperature scaling or other calibration can help under appropriate validation, but should be fitted on separate data and does not correct wrong class rankings by itself.

**Technical details and references.**

Accuracy considers only which class has the largest probability; cross-entropy also measures confidence. A few increasingly confident mistakes can dominate average negative log likelihood even as more borderline examples become correctly classified. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html) [2](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html)

$$\mathcal L_i=-\log p(y_i\mid x_i).$$

Changing a wrong example's true-class probability from 0.1 to 0.001 increases its loss from about 2.30 to 6.91 without changing its correctness. Inspect confidence distributions, loss by slice, reliability diagrams, and mislabeled/outlier examples. Select checkpoints according to the actual deployment objective; probability-sensitive decisions may prefer lower log loss. Temperature scaling fitted on separate validation data can improve calibration, but cannot fix incorrect rankings or data leakage.
